pages.title: About Me
pages.body: ## Security rarely fails because of lack of equipment or procedures. It fails because decisions are made too late, by people too far from the threat. This understanding defines how I work. ## Where I Come From I began my career in a special operations unit, where security decisions had real consequences for every mission. Early exposure to real threats shaped my understanding of risk, uncertainty, and consequence—long before I entered corporate or project environments. ## How My Work Evolved As my work moved from direct execution to leadership and advisory roles, I repeatedly observed the same pattern: Security systems failed because their designs assumed ideal operating conditions. This led me to focus on security architecture, governance, and decision support across the full operation. ## How I Think About Security I do not treat security as a product, a checklist, or a certification exercise. I view it as a dynamic system under stress, shaped by leadership behavior, information flow, and decision timing. If a system cannot function when pressure increases, it is not secure. ## Professional Boundaries I work with organisations that treat security as a leadership responsibility embedded in operational decisions. I decline work where risk is acknowledged rhetorically but ignored operationally. ## Professional Qualifications & Certifications - UN Department of Safety and Security (UNDSS) – BSAFE, Information Security, Active Shooter - U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) & FEMA – Terrorism & Explosive Threat Frameworks - Texas A&M / Homeland Security – THIRA, WMD Terrorism, Active Attack Leadership - Certified Security Evaluation Engineer (Level II), PRC - Senior Security & Protection Systems Engineer, MIIT - Security Industry Authority (UK) – Counter Terrorism ## My role is to help organizations operate where assumptions fail and consequences are real.

pages.title: Experience
pages.body: ## Experience Is Only Valuable When It Has Been Tested I do not present experience as a list of roles or dates. I present it as systems designed, decisions made, and consequences managed under real-world pressure. My work spans high-risk regions, complex political environments, and projects where security failure would directly impact lives, operations, or national-level interests. ## High-Risk Mining & Resource Projects I have led and advised security systems for mining operations in extremely high-risk regions, including Balochistan, where armed groups, political volatility, and terrain constraints intersect. My work focused on: - Camp, mine, and remote water source protection - Armed force coordination and layered defense models - Movement security and emergency evacuation planning Security design was integrated with production rhythms and cost control, not imposed as an external burden. ## Energy, Power & Critical Infrastructure For large-scale energy and power infrastructure projects in Africa and South Asia, I supported security governance covering tens of thousands of personnel. Key challenges included: - Open construction environments - Multi-subcontractor coordination - Community tension and political sensitivity The security architecture integrated prevention, early warning, rapid decision escalation and practical on-site protection. ## Urban Fixed-Site Protection In high-threat urban environments such as Baghdad, I contributed to fixed-site protection models where threats were dynamic and intelligence-driven. This work required: - Adaptive access control and perimeter design - Intelligence-informed security postures - Coordination with local authorities and international stakeholders The goal was continuity of operation, not fortress-style isolation. ## Large-Scale EPC & Mobile Operations I have supported EPC projects involving large-scale personnel movement across long distances and unstable regions. Focus areas included: - Route risk assessment and convoy planning - Mobile security governance - Incident response and escalation protocols Security planning was aligned with logistics reality, not ideal assumptions. ## How I Work in Practice Across these domains, my role typically involves: - Translating threat reality into actionable security architecture - Supporting leadership decision-making under uncertainty - Integrating security with operations, cost, and schedule - Preventing security from becoming a symbolic or cosmetic function ## Experience matters only when it survives pressure. ## Footprints ### Overseas EPC Projects \| High-Risk Regions \| Security Chief Engineer --- AUIB Hospital Project – Baghdad, Iraq Baltic Gas Chemical Complex (GCC), Russia Bangladesh GF Chemical Plant SHEMAL 2×350MW Thermal Power Plant – Mosul, Iraq Najibiyah 2×125MW Gas Power Plant Conversion Project – Iraq Zubair Gas Power Plant Conversion Project – Basra, Iraq Boduakali 1320MW (2×660MW) Coal-Fired Power Plant – Bangladesh Award:2023 Outstanding Overseas Security Practice Award Central Myanmar Solar PV Cluster Project Shakshuk 300MW Solar Power Plant – Libya Boffa Chalco Bauxite Mine Project – Guinea Award:2022 Outstanding Overseas Security Practice Award ### National-Level Risk Assessments \| Strategic Infrastructure \| Security Audits --- China Energy Engineering Group Overseas Social Security Risk Assessment Project SCADA & Metering System Phase III – Pakistan National Transmission Company (NTDC) Nigeria Dangote Petroleum Refinery Project Nigeria KOGI Cement plant Nigeria EDO-3 Cement plant Kyaukpyu 135MW Gas Power Plant – Myanmar Barisal 350MW Coal-Fired Power Plant – Bangladesh COVID-19 Pandemic Government PPE Procurement & Airlift Operations Embassy of Pakistan & High-Security Facility Projects Embassy in Egypt – Security System Upgrade ### Technical Security Engineering Experience & Professional Skills --- Kunlun Hotel Auction Event – Beijing CRCC Fangshan Bridge Factory – Beijing SOKOTO Cement Production Line Project – Nigeria Gwadar 300MW Coal-Fired Power Plant – Pakistan ### National-Level Security Operations --- 70th Anniversary National Day Low-Altitude Security Mission

pages.title: Contact
pages.body:
RAVEN / CONTACT

# Discuss your project [longbow.msu@gmail.com →](mailto:longbow.msu@gmail.com) --- ## When to Contact When security is mission-critical, and assumptions are likely to fail, I provide advisory support, security architecture design, and decision-level consultation. This page is intended for organizations and leaders operating in hostile or unstable environments. ## Engagement Scope I typically engage in: - High-risk project security architecture and governance - Protective security and PSD advisory - Crisis response and evacuation decision support - Armed force coordination frameworks - Security audits and vulnerability assessments for complex operations If your requirement is cosmetic security or low-risk coverage, I may not be the right fit. ## How to Engage For serious inquiries, please provide: - Organization or project context - Operating region and threat environment - Scope of advisory or security requirement - Preferred engagement model (advisory, design, audit, training) This allows me to assess feasibility and alignment before responding. ## Contact Details Email: [longbow.msu@gmail.com](mailto:longbow.msu@gmail.com) Response time varies depending on operational commitments. I work with organizations that understand security is a leadership responsibility, not a procurement checkbox. I decline engagements where risk is acknowledged rhetorically but ignored operationally. ## Security decisions define outcomes long before incidents occur.

pages.title: Training
pages.body: # HEAT — Hostile Environment Awareness Training 10 modules · 80 lessons · Scenario exercises and final assessment Free online learning · No registration or app required [Open course directory \| Path, progress and templates](https://ravenlong-heat-directory.vercel.app/en/)　[Start Module 01](https://www.ravenlong.com/p/3f93102210ef81caad2eff6c4b83d5f5) Purpose: Prepare business travellers, tourists, short-term visitors, field researchers and operational personnel entering hostile environments to recognise danger, protect themselves, and respond to detention, violence, lost contact or restricted medical care. This course teaches personal safety in places affected by conflict, unrest and serious security threats. Someone may be visiting a historic site, attending a meeting or inspecting a remote project. Their safety questions are much harder: what if security forces take them away without a clear process? What if unrest blocks the hotel entrance? What if an armed checkpoint seizes their documents, or an injured companion cannot reach medical care? The course teaches practical protective decisions under those conditions. HEAT helps ordinary travellers and field visitors to recognise a threat, understand the immediate danger, take protective action, stop unsafe work and decide when activity can safely resume. Read the author's note Danger does not follow the order of a manual. A normal working day can be interrupted by gunfire. People may be confronted before they understand what is happening. Professional medical help might be unavailable for hours. People need specific actions: how to reduce exposure, when to move, when to stop the task, and whether the place they occupy still offers protection. Some subjects need a complete incident narrative; others need a comparison of choices or a field tool learners can actually use. The important thing is to understand why an action works, when it would fail, and what to do as circumstances changeand put the lesson into practice. — Raven --- ## Who this is for The primary audience is business travellers, tourists, short-term visitors, journalists and field researchers who must enter areas affected by conflict, civil unrest, serious crime or limited emergency services. Construction, mining, energy, humanitarian and other operational personnel are also included. The lessons work for people travelling independently or with a small group, as well as those supported by a professional team. The course covers hostile behaviour, confrontational inspections, threats from crowds and gunfire, explosive hazards, compound and worksite safety, coercion, detention, medical emergencies and evacuation. Hands-on first aid, protective driving and specialist security interventions require supervised training. The course keeps the non-specialist's actions and limits clear. ## One connected learning sequence Phase 1 \| Prepare (01–02): Understand threats, define limits for the activity and prepare essential protective resources. Phase 2 \| Move and operate (03–06): Develop awareness and manage encounters at hotels, historic sites, public transport, meetings, inspection visits and work locations. Phase 3 \| Respond (07–10): Respond to violence, unrest, explosives, coercion, detention and injuries; select shelter, assistance or evacuation as required. Lesson 11 \| Integrated review: Apply these skills to a developing field-operation scenario before the 50-question final assessment. ## What you should be able to do - Gunfire nearby: Reduce exposure immediately. Seek genuine protection without approaching the sound. - Confrontational checkpoint: Keep your hands and movements visible; avoid sudden movements or escalating the argument. - Threat to a worksite: Suspend exposed work. Move people into a protected area and reassess operations. - Suspicious explosive item: Do not touch or investigate it. Withdraw and leave it to specialists. - Seriously injured colleague: Check scene safety, recognise urgent symptoms and seek medical support. - Threat to a compound: Choose sheltering, local relocation or evacuation according to actual conditions. The assessment focuses on whether you know what is happening, what to do first and what action would make it worse. --- ## Start here \| Ten modules and a review Use the [interactive course directory](https://ravenlong-heat-directory.vercel.app/en/) to choose a module, see estimated study times, save progress in your browser and download field templates. The original direct module links remain below. 01 \| Hostile Environments and Main Threats 02 \| Preparing for High-Risk Operations 03 \| Situational Awareness and Personal Security 04 \| Cultural Awareness, Communication, and De-escalation 05 \| Movement and Vehicle Safety in High-Risk Areas 06 \| Accommodation, Public Venues and Site Protection 07 \| Armed Violence, Civil Unrest and Explosive Hazards 08 \| Kidnapping Prevention, Detention, and Survival 09 \| Emergency Medical Action and Stress in Hostile Environments 10 \| Emergency Communications, Crisis Response, and Evacuation 11 \| Course Review and Key Takeaways --- ## Study and assessment After each module, try the scenario exercise or optional planning card, then take the 15-question scored quiz. After the ten modules and Section 11 review, take the final assessment. A score of at least 40/50 passes. The results page explains how to email a screenshot showing your name, score and date. I will review it and send your electronic certificate. Final assessment \| 50 questions ## Certificate preview Formal HEAT certificate preview The electronic certificate issued after a pass is verified will include your name, completion date and certificate ID. ## Social media posters [View and save the Chinese and English posters](https://www.ravenlong.com/p/3fa3102210ef81c087f4d267b829f1e9) Travelling Without Cell Service: Satellite Communication & Check-in Plan \| HEAT Field Guide
